items.title: Interest costs on global government debt have never been higher: Gross interest expenditure among OECD countries surged +$180 billion YoY in 2025, to a record $2.24 trillion. This marks the 4th consecutive annual increase, totaling +$960 billion. The US accounted for ~65% of the total, at $1.45 trillion, while the EU represented ~18%, or $400 billion. As a % of global GDP, gross interest costs stood at ~3.2% last year, their 2nd-highest level in at least 20 years. Meanwhile, OECD countries are estimated to borrow another $18 trillion in 2026, the highest annual total on record. The global debt crisis is spiraling out of control.
items.content:
Interest costs on global government debt have never been higher:

Gross interest expenditure among OECD countries surged +$180 billion YoY in 2025, to a record $2.24 trillion.

This marks the 4th consecutive annual increase, totaling +$960 billion.

The US accounted for ~65% of the total, at $1.45 trillion, while the EU represented ~18%, or $400 billion.

As a % of global GDP, gross interest costs stood at ~3.2% last year, their 2nd-highest level in at least 20 years.

Meanwhile, OECD countries are estimated to borrow another $18 trillion in 2026, the highest annual total on record.

The global debt crisis is spiraling out of control.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 11, 2026

items.title: BREAKING: The US Debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to rise to a record 156% in 2050, according to the CBO's latest forecast. That would mark a +57 percentage point increase from the current ~99%. At the same time, the Treasury Department estimates the ratio will surge to a massive 213% over the same period, or 57 percentage points higher than the CBO's estimate. Furthermore, neither estimate includes intragovernmental debt, such as Treasury securities held by Social Security and other federal trust funds. The worst part? Both forecasts assume the US avoids a recession during this entire period. US debt could be heading in a far worse direction than forecasts suggest.

items.title: The shift we are seeing right now is extraordinary. Markets now see a BASE case of 4 interest rate hikes by July 2027. To put this into perspective, at the start of 2026, markets saw 4 interest rate CUTS during this time period. That's a difference of +200 basis points between interest rate expectations now and 9 months ago. These are, by far, the most hawkish Fed policy expectations since the Fed began raising interest rates in March 2022. It's clear: the market believes "higher for longer" is back and inflation is here to stay. Wednesday is going to be an eventful day.

items.content:
US companies are borrowing at a rapid pace in Europe:

US corporates have raised €149 billion, or $173 billion, in European bonds so far in 2026, the 2nd-highest annual total on record.

This is also double the full-year amount seen in 2022 and 2023.

At this pace, US firms are set to borrow a record €225 billion, or $261 billion, this year.

This comes as heavy AI-related borrowing from Big Tech has crowded the US Dollar bond market, leaving other issuers facing worse pricing and less room to raise debt domestically.

Euro-denominated debt is also cheaper to service for high-grade borrowers than US Dollar debt, a key advantage for global companies earning revenue in Euros.

US firms are increasingly looking abroad for financing as the US market can no longer easily absorb the debt wave.
— The Kobeissi Letter (@KobeissiLetter) Sep 11, 2026

items.content:
US housing affordability is rapidly deteriorating:

The annual income needed to afford an average home in the US surged +$4,107 in May, to a record $124,674 per year.

This marks the 3rd consecutive monthly increase, totaling +$9,734.

By comparison, US median household income stands at $86,159 per year.

This brings the gap between median household income and the income needed to afford an average home to $38,515, the largest gap since July 2025.

This is just $2,288 below the $40,803 record set in June 2024.

To put this into perspective, median household income was $5,139 higher than the income required to buy a home in 2021.

Homeownership is becoming increasingly out of reach for the average American.

items.title: BREAKING: US ETFs attracted +$180 billion in inflows in August, the 6th-largest monthly inflow on record. This was driven by equity ETFs, which posted +$100 billion in inflows. This also follows +$190 billion in total inflows in July and +$220 billion in June. In the first 8 months of 2026, US ETFs have seen +$1.4 trillion in inflows, on track for their largest annual intake on record. Equity funds accounted for ~63%, or +$880 billion, of the total. Investor risk appetite remains incredibly strong.

items.title: Leveraged funds are becoming increasingly bearish on US tech: Leveraged fund short positions on Nasdaq 100 futures are up to ~$75 billion, near their highest in at least 4 years. Short positioning has more than doubled since February. Meanwhile, long positioning on Nasdaq 100 futures is down to ~$18 billion, its lowest since mid-2025. As a result, net positioning among leveraged funds is down to -$57 billion, near its lowest since at least 2022. This marks a sharp reversal from the positive net positioning recorded in November 2025. Leveraged funds are increasingly betting against tech stocks.
